facts.fact_text: At the time of the events giving rise to the present application, the applicant was the head of the Batman branch of the People's Democratic Party (DEHAP).
Subsequently, the applicant was the head of the Batman branch of the Party for a Democratic Society (DTP).

When questioned on 18 October 2005, the applicant was asked about his participation in an event commemorating a number of deceased members of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party, an illegal armed organisation) held on 22 August 2005.
The applicant responded that he had become aware of the event commemorating deceased PKK members when demonstrators had started to march to the cemetery where the deceased were buried.

The applicant stated that, as he was the head of the Batman branch of DEHAP (People's Democratic Party), he had attended the march in order to keep the demonstrators under control and to prevent any possible disturbances in the town.

The applicant stated that he had participated in several demonstrations and readings of press statements in his capacity as the head of the Batman branch of DEHAP (People's Democratic Party) and the DTP (Party for a Democratic Society).
The applicant contended that he had attended the demonstrations and meetings in question in order to control the crowds and to prevent any possible disturbances.
The applicant claimed that his aim was to contribute to peace and democracy.
On 23 March 2006, the applicant was brought before the Batman Magistrates' Court and questioned in respect of his involvement in a demonstration held on 16 February 2006 in Batman.

The applicant submitted that he had attended the demonstration of 16 February 2006 with a view to preventing violence, since he was the head of the DTP (Party for a Democratic Society) at the material time.
In the indictment, the Diyarbakır public prosecutor listed a total of ten marches and demonstrations which the applicant had attended.
The applicant stated that although he had participated in the public meetings indicated in the indictment, he had not chanted any slogans or carried banners containing illegal expressions.
The applicant submitted that he had not directed demonstrators to commit any illegal acts.

The applicant stressed that in general he attended such public meetings at the request of the security forces, since the security forces asked him to be present in order to prevent any possible clashes between themselves and the demonstrators.

In his defence submissions before the Diyarbakır Assize Court, the applicant stated that he had participated in the demonstrations and the reading out of press statements mentioned in the indictment but that he had neither chanted slogans nor carried banners.

The applicant submitted before the Diyarbakır Assize Court that he had attended those meetings at the request of the security forces and that the security forces had asked him to warn the crowds not to resist them and to work with them with a view to preventing possible disturbances.
The Batman Magistrates' Court ordered the applicant's remand in custody.

On 26 September 2006, the Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant and his co-accused M.G. of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 7 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.
The applicant was sentenced to six years and three months' imprisonment by the Diyarbakır Assize Court.
The Diyarbakır Assize Court decided to convict the applicant and M.G. under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).
On 13 April 2010, the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance judgment of the Diyarbakır Assize Court.
On 16 August 2012, the Diyarbakır Assize Court decided to reduce the applicant's sentence to five years, two months and fifteen days' imprisonment.

On 26 September 2006, the Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant and his co-accused M.G. of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 7 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.

The Diyarbakır Assize Court considered that, taking into account the continuity and nature of the applicant's and M.G.'s acts, those acts went beyond the offence of dissemination of propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation and amounted to the offence of 'knowingly and willingly aiding an illegal organisation without being in the hierarchical structure' proscribed by Article 220 § 7 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

At the material time, Article 220 § 7 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who aids an illegal organisation knowingly and willingly, even if he does not belong to the hierarchical structure of the organisation, shall be punished as a member of the organisation.

Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who becomes a member of an armed organisation mentioned in Article 314 § 1 shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and ten years.

Article 314 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that other provisions relating to the crime of establishing an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity are also applicable to the crime of membership of an armed organisation.

At its 106th plenary session, held on 11 and 12 March 2016, the Venice Commission (European Commission for Democracy through Law) adopted an Opinion on Articles 216, 299, 301 and 314 of the Penal Code of Turkey (CDL-AD(2016)002).
The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that the Penal Code of Turkey does not contain a definition of an armed organisation or an armed group.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that the Court of Cassation of Turkey developed the criterion of 'membership' in an armed organisation by examining different acts of the suspect, taking account of their 'continuity, diversity and intensity', in order to determine whether those acts prove an 'organic relationship' with the organisation or whether the acts may be considered as committed knowingly and wilfully within the 'hierarchical structure' of the organisation.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that if the 'organic relationship' with the organisation cannot be proven on the basis of acts attributed to the defendant which do not present any 'continuity, diversity or intensity', the paragraphs on 'aiding and abetting an armed organisation' or 'committing crime on behalf of an armed organisation' under Article 220 of the Penal Code may be applied.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that, according to non-governmental sources, in the application of Article 314 of the Penal Code of Turkey, domestic courts in many cases decide on the membership of a person in an armed organisation on the basis of very weak evidence, raising questions as to the 'foreseeability' of the application of Article 314.

The Venice Commission's Opinion stated that conviction on the basis of weak evidence in the application of Article 314 of the Penal Code of Turkey may create problems in the field of Article 7 of the Convention, since that provision embodies the principle that criminal law must not be extensively construed to an accused's detriment.

The Venice Commission's Opinion stated that where the only evidence which led domestic courts to convict a defendant for being a member of an armed organisation consists of forms of expression, reliance on weak evidence may also give rise to problems concerning the 'foreseeability' of the interference with the right to freedom of expression.

The Venice Commission stated that the loose application of the criteria of 'continuity, diversity and intensity' may give rise to issues concerning the principle of legality within the meaning of Article 7 of the Convention.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that Article 220(7) of the Penal Code of Turkey, concerning aiding and abetting an organisation knowingly and willingly, was also applied to cases involving freedom of expression.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that defendants who are considered to have committed crimes on behalf of an armed organisation under paragraph 6 of Article 220 of the Penal Code, or to have aided and abetted an armed organisation knowingly and willingly under paragraph 7 of Article 220, are also sentenced for the offence of being a member of that organisation under Article 314, although their 'organic relationship' with the armed organisation cannot be proven.

Mr Thomas Hammarberg considered that the provisions contained in the Turkish anti-terror legislation and Article 220 of the Turkish Criminal Code allow for a very wide margin of appreciation, in particular in cases where membership in a terrorist organisation has not been proven and when an act or statement may be deemed to coincide with the aims or instructions of a terrorist organisation.

The Human Rights Watch report stated that legal amendments since 2005, along with case law since 2008, have allowed courts in Turkey to convict demonstrators under the harshest terrorism laws by invoking Articles 220 and 314 of the Turkish Penal Code in combination with the Anti-Terror Law (Law no. 3713).

The Human Rights Watch report stated that Turkish Penal Code Articles 220/6 and 220/7 are so vaguely worded and lacking in clarity about what is prohibited as to offer an individual no indication of how to regulate or limit conduct.

Human Rights Watch recommended that the Turkish Government urgently amend Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code and repeal Articles 220/6 and 220/7, which are vague, lack legal clarity and specificity, and are therefore subject to arbitrary application.
The Amnesty International report stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code is often used to prosecute conduct protected by the rights to freedom of expression, association and assembly.

The Amnesty International report stated that the choice of prosecutors to prosecute under Article 220/6 or Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code often appears arbitrary, with similar behaviour sometimes prosecuted under one, sometimes under the other, and sometimes under Article 314 directly.

The Batman public prosecutor held that the offence which the applicant had committed, namely membership of a terrorist organisation and carrying out membership activities, was not within the Batman public prosecutor's office's jurisdiction.

The Diyarbakır public prosecutor charged the applicant and a certain M.G. under Article 220 § 8 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) with disseminating propaganda in favour of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) on ten occasions.

The Diyarbakır public prosecutor alleged that the events attended by the applicant had been organised either in line with the policies of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) or under its instructions with a view to supporting that organisation.

The Diyarbakır public prosecutor asked the Diyarbakır Assize Court to convict the applicant under Articles 220 § 7 and 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) of membership of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party).
The Diyarbakır Assize Court found that all of the marches and demonstrations were organised in line with the 'Democratic Political Struggle' strategy adopted by the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party).

The Diyarbakır Assize Court found that the applicant and M.G. organised several illegal demonstrations in line with the PKK's (Kurdish Workers' Party) instructions and that during those demonstrations they addressed demonstrators who chanted slogans and carried banners containing expressions in favour of the PKK and Abdullah Öcalan.

The applicant stated that, as he was the head of the Batman branch of DEHAP (People's Democratic Party), he had attended the march in order to keep the demonstrators under control and to prevent any possible disturbances in the town.

The applicant stated that his intention had been to express the social fact that Abdullah Öcalan was regarded as a political actor by the local population, and that he was against any kind of violence.

When the Batman public prosecutor reminded the applicant of the violent acts of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party), the applicant stated that he was against violence regardless of whom it emanated from.
The applicant stated that he had not committed any offence during the demonstrations and readings of press statements he attended.

When asked about a sentence condemning both the death of Turkish soldiers and PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) members which he had uttered during a speech, the applicant stated that he would utter that sentence again without hesitation.
The applicant contended that he had attended the demonstrations and meetings in question in order to control the crowds and to prevent any possible disturbances.
The applicant claimed that his aim was to contribute to peace and democracy.
The applicant stated that although he had participated in the public meetings indicated in the indictment, he had not chanted any slogans or carried banners containing illegal expressions.
The applicant submitted that he had not directed demonstrators to commit any illegal acts.

The applicant stressed that in general he attended such public meetings at the request of the security forces, since the security forces asked him to be present in order to prevent any possible clashes between themselves and the demonstrators.
The applicant was sentenced to six years and three months' imprisonment by the Diyarbakır Assize Court.

In his defence submissions before the Diyarbakır Assize Court, the applicant stated that he had participated in the demonstrations and the reading out of press statements mentioned in the indictment but that he had neither chanted slogans nor carried banners.

The applicant submitted before the Diyarbakır Assize Court that he had attended those meetings at the request of the security forces and that the security forces had asked him to warn the crowds not to resist them and to work with them with a view to preventing possible disturbances.

The Diyarbakır Assize Court found the applicant's defence submissions — that his aim had been to prevent clashes between demonstrators and security forces and that he had not intended to disseminate propaganda in favour of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) — to be baseless.

The Diyarbakır Assize Court considered that, taking into account the continuity and nature of the applicant's and M.G.'s acts, those acts went beyond the offence of dissemination of propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation and amounted to the offence of 'knowingly and willingly aiding an illegal organisation without being in the hierarchical structure' proscribed by Article 220 § 7 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that Amnesty International, in its 2013 Report on Turkey, considered that conduct which is not in itself criminal — such as activity related to the exercise of the rights to freedom of assembly, association and expression — is considered as evidence of membership of defendants in an armed organisation, and that individuals have been prosecuted for membership of a terrorist organisation on charges relating solely to their engagement in peaceful and lawful pro-Kurdish activities.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that examples of concrete cases provided by Amnesty International in which evidence was considered to link defendants to a terrorist organisation included attendance at six different demonstrations allegedly organised by a terrorist organisation and a speech made at one of those demonstrations, or participation in the 'Political Academy' organised by the Peace and Democracy Party (BDP) and diverse activities in the framework of that Academy.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that in the case of Yılmaz and Kılıç v. Turkey (application no. 68514/01), the European Court of Human Rights considered that where the only evidence which led to the criminal conviction of the applicants under Article 169 of the former Penal Code was forms of expression, it should be concluded that there was an interference with the applicants' right to freedom of expression.

The Venice Commission's Opinion noted that the European Court of Human Rights applied the same principle in the case of Gül and others v. Turkey (application no. 4870/02) and held that the criminal conviction of the applicants on the basis of Article 169 of the former Penal Code constituted an interference with their right to freedom of expression, since the only evidence used against them was the content of the slogans they shouted during a public demonstration.

The Venice Commission recommended that the expression of an opinion in its different forms should not be the only evidence before domestic courts to decide on the membership of a defendant in an armed organisation.

The Venice Commission stated that where the only evidence consists of forms of expression, a conviction for being a member of an armed organisation would constitute an interference with the right to freedom of expression, and that the necessity of this interference should be examined in the concrete circumstances of each case on the basis of the criteria set forth in the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights, in particular the criterion of 'incitement to violence'.

Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that violence or the threat to use violence is an essential component of an act of terrorism, and that restrictions of human rights in the fight against terrorism must be defined as precisely as possible and be necessary and proportionate to the aim pursued.

The Human Rights Watch report stated that many hundreds of people in Turkey face prosecution or are serving substantial sentences for terrorism convictions for engaging in peaceful protest or throwing stones or burning a tire at a protest.

The Amnesty International report stated that when prosecutors seek to convict a person under Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code, they often do not provide evidence demonstrating a link to a terrorist organisation, nor do they attempt to prove that the accused was engaged in any criminal offence or in aiding and abetting, other than supposedly assisting the proscribed organisation.

Amnesty International stated that no inference should be drawn from someone undertaking a lawful act — such as participating in a peaceful demonstration — even if such acts benefit, through lawful means, goals shared by a terrorist organisation, and that anyone carrying out a lawful act which does not aid and abet the planning or commission of a crime should not be criminalised on the sole basis of their political convictions.
